subject: Request: Alignment on streaming vs sync commitments — TTFT and sustained tokens/sec
messages:
From: Naomi Feldman <naomi.feldman@redwood.com>
To: Alex Porter <alex.porter@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 11 Jul 2028 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: Request: Alignment on streaming vs sync commitments — TTFT and sustained tokens/sec

Alex —

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we continue towards contract language, procurement has asked us to clarify an operational carveout for streaming endpoints vs synchronous endpoints. Specifically they want to see: time-to-first-token (TTFT) targets and sustained token/sec expectations for our streaming API, and the operational fallback if we can’t meet those at peak.

High level ask from Acme procurement: they need a short, machine-readable appendix that specifies:
- TTFT target (P95) for streaming (for 2–8k token outputs)
- Sustained tokens/sec expectation per customer connection (and per endpoint)
- What constitutes a breach vs a temporary degradation (and observable signals)
- Fallback behavior (automatic downgrade to smaller model, delayed buffering, or sync fallback)

Can you confirm what we can commit to for a pilot (90-day) and what would be an exception requiring engineering sign-off? I’m attaching the traffic sample they shared in the discovery call so you can see the burst profile.

Attachments: acme-traffic-sample-6h.csv

Thanks,
Naomi Feldman
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
naomi.feldman@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0192

--
Redwood Inference — Production-first LLM inference

Subject: Re: Request: Alignment on streaming vs sync commitments — TTFT and sustained tokens/sec

Naomi —

Appreciate the quick follow-up. I’ve attached the 6-hour token profile from our staging traffic (same file you got). A couple of clarifying points from our side:
- The most critical part for the compliance team is TTFT for streaming (they consider anything over 300ms at P95 to be a blocker for our real-time clinician UI).
- Sustained tokens/sec: during business hours the average per-connection sustained rate is ~40 tokens/sec with bursts up to 220 tokens/sec for short periods (~20–45s).
- If you can’t hit the TTFT target during bursts we would like to understand the precise fallback (e.g., shorter context window model, partial acceptance of sync endpoints, or queuing).

Procurement would like the appendix to explicitly state the carveouts you would need (e.g., customer-specific throughput caps, pilot as non-production, or explicit exceptions when network/hardware constraints exist).

Attachments: acme-traffic-sample-6h.csv

Cheers,
Alex Porter

Subject: Re: Request: Alignment on streaming vs sync commitments — TTFT and sustained tokens/sec

Hi all —

Thanks for the data, Alex. We reviewed the sample and sketched a conservative pilot commitment that keeps both reliability and cost containment in mind. Summary proposal (pilot: 90 days):

1) TTFT (streaming) — Pilot target: P95 <= 350ms for outputs <= 4k tokens; for outputs 4k–8k target P95 <= 500ms.
   - Exception: during platform-wide burst events (top 0.5% of traffic by volume) the TTFT may slip and will be classified as "degradation" not "breach" if we notify and enable fallback.

2) Sustained tokens/sec per connection — We can commit to a sustained 40 tokens/sec (P90) per connection. Short bursts up to 200–220 tokens/sec for 15–60s are supported but will be treated as transient and subject to rate shaping if they coincide with cluster-wide saturation.

3) Fallback options (ordered):
   a) Automatic prefix/KV cache hot-path routing to reduce TTFT latency where cache coverage is high.
   b) Transparent model variant fallback (e.g., same-architecture 8-bit quant variant) when throughput demands exceed committed sustained rate.
   c) Sync fallback: if streaming cannot sustain TTFT after 30s of shaping, we can switch the request to a synchronous endpoint with a documented response-time SLA.

4) Observability & Signals — We will provide a shared dashboard with: P50/P95 TTFT, per-connection tokens/sec, cluster saturation (% free worker slots), and an alert when rate shaping is engaged. These metrics will be visible to Acme during pilot.

5) Exceptions requiring engineering sign-off — sustained >200 tokens/sec averaged over a 5-minute window per connection, or any repeatable TTFT >1s at P95 for the same workload.

Attached: redwood-ttft-proposal-v1.pdf (formal appendix language + example SLA table).

If this looks acceptable as a pilot commitment, we can turn the appendix into contract language for procurement and include the observability links for operational review.

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Director, Strategic Accounts — Redwood Inference
karthik.iyer@redwood.com | +1 (650) 555-0124

Folks —

Reviewed and approve in principle. A few contractual clarifications we need before procurement signs:

1) Wording: classify two classes of operational state in the appendix — "Normal" (we meet TTFT and sustained targets) and "Degraded" (we fall back to rate shaping/model-variant/sync fallback). Only "Degraded" states can trigger the exception carveout; explicit examples should be included (network partition, cluster-wide burst, or regional hardware failure).

2) Billing: make clear that degraded-mode routing that uses heavier compute (e.g., model duplication for redundancy) will be billable at agreed rates in the appendix.

3) Measurement window: pilot SLO measurement period = 14 days after pilot ramp, with P95 calculated over business-hours traffic.

4) Deliverables before procurement sign-off: shared dashboard link, alert sample, and the explicit gating criteria for pilot parity. Please add these as checklist items in the appendix.

Alex — Naomi, Karthik, can you confirm you’ll deliver the dashboard + alert sample by next Wednesday (2028-07-20)? Procurement needs that date for their timeline.

Marissa Cole
VP, Sales Operations — Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com
